claim: Vangl2 mRNA level is increased in PBMCs from sepsis patients compared to healthy controls.
source: Transcription levels of Vangl2 in PBMCs from healthy volunteers (healthy control, HC) and sepsis patients were analyzed by real-time PCR (n = 8).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data from patient samples shown in Figure 1A

claim: The serum of the high Vangl2 expression group had lower levels of IL-6, white blood cell, and acute C-reactive protein than the low Vangl2 expression group.
source: Moreover, the serum of the high Vangl2 expression group had lower levels of IL-6, white blood cell, and acute C-reactive protein than the low Vangl2 expression group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by clinical measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Vangl2 is upregulated at both mRNA and protein levels after LPS stimulation in BMDMs, neutrophils, and peritoneal macrophages.
source: Moreover, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and western blot analyses revealed strong upregulation of Vangl2 at both the mRNA and protein levels after LPS stimulation in bone marrow (BM)-derived macrophages (BMDMs), neutrophils, and peritoneal macrophages (pMACs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1E), suggesting that Vangl2 is induced in immune organ tissues and cells in response to inflammation.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–1E

claim: All Vangl2ΔM mice died after LPS-induced septic shock within 20 hr, compared to only 20% of the WT mice.
source: We found that all Vangl2ΔM mice died after LPS-induced septic shock within 20 hr, compared to only 20% of the WT mice, whereas the remaining WT mice survived for more than 50 hr (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Vangl2ΔM mice markedly increased the protein level of IL-1β in isolated CD11b+ splenocytes.
source: Consistent with this observation, Vangl2ΔM mice markedly increased the protein level of IL-1β in isolated CD11b+ splenocytes (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Vangl2ΔM mice showed markedly elevated mRNA levels of Il1b, Tnfa and Il6 in the spleen after LPS treatment.
source: and mRNA levels of Il1b, Tnfa and Il6 in the spleen (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Vangl2ΔM mice showed markedly elevated serum amounts of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 after LPS treatment, compared with WT mice.
source: Meanwhile, Vangl2ΔM mice showed markedly elevated serum amounts of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6 after LPS treatment, compared with WT mice (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Myeloid cell-specific deletion of Vangl2 in mice enhances the sensitivity and severity of LPS-induced septic shock.
source: Together, these data provide in vivo evidence that myeloid cell-specific deletion of Vangl2 in mice enhances the sensitivity and severity of LPS-induced septic shock and is associated with increased expression of proinflammatory cytokines.
evidence: Inferred from survival data and cytokine measurements in Vangl2ΔM mice

claim: RNA-seq analysis identified 907 upregulated genes (including inflammatory cytokines) and 1092 downregulated genes in response to Vangl2 deficiency in BMDMs after LPS stimulation.
source: Results showed 907 upregulated genes (including inflammatory cytokines) and 1092 downregulated genes in response to Vangl2 deficiency in BMDMs after LPS stimulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Genes involved in TNF signaling pathway and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction were highly enriched in Vangl2ΔM BMDMs after LPS stimulation.
source: Moreover, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) analysis revealed genes involved in TNF signaling pathway and cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction were highly enriched in Vangl2ΔM BMDMs after LPS stimulation, suggesting that Vangl2 may regulate these signaling pathways and related cytokines release (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by KEGG analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: Phosphorylations of p65 were enhanced and remained high level for a sustained period in Vangl2-deficient pMACs and neutrophils, compared with WT cells.
source: We found that phosphorylations of p65 were enhanced and remained high level for a sustained period in Vangl2-deficient pMACs and neutrophils, compared with WT cells (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2A–D

claim: Vangl2-deficient macrophages and neutrophils showed markedly elevated proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 after LPS treatment.
source: Consistent with this observation, Vangl2-deficient macrophages, and neutrophils showed markedly elevated proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-6 (Figure 2E, F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E), and IL-1β (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F), after LPS treatment.
evidence: Supported by qPCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 2E, F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E, F

claim: Enhanced p65 nuclear accumulation was detected in LPS-induced Vangl2-deficient neutrophils, compared with WT neutrophils.
source: Moreover, we detected enhanced p65 nuclear accumulation in LPS-induced Vangl2-deficient neutrophils, compared with WT neutrophils (Figure 2G, H).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2G, H

claim: Vangl2 overexpression inhibited phosphorylation of p65 in A549 cells.
source: To further confirm the function of Vangl2 in regulating NF-κB signaling, we overexpressed Flag-tagged Vangl2 in A549 cells. We found that Vangl2 overexpression inhibited phosphorylation of p65 in A549 cells (Figure 2I, J).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2I, J

claim: Vangl2 prevents LPS-induced NF-κB activation and proinflammatory cytokine production.
source: These results suggest that Vangl2 prevents LPS-induced NF-κB activation and proinflammatory cytokine production.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing Vangl2 deficiency increases NF-κB activation and cytokine production

claim: Vangl2 markedly inhibited NF-κB activation induced by LPS, IL-1β, or TNF-α in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We found that Vangl2 markedly inhibited NF-κB activation induced by LPS, IL-1β, or TNF-α in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3A–C

claim: NF-κB-luc activity was strongly activated by overexpression of MyD88, IRAK1, TRAF6, IKKα, IKKβ, or p65, but all of these activities were inhibited when Vangl2 was co-transfected at increasing concentrations.
source: NF-κB-luc activity was strongly activated by overexpression of MyD88, IRAK1, TRAF6, IKKα, IKKβ, or p65, but all of these activities were inhibited when Vangl2 was co-transfected at increasing concentrations (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F), suggesting that Vangl2 may block NF-κB activation at the very downstream signaling level of p65.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F

claim: Vangl2 interacted strongly with IKKα, IKKβ, p65, and MyD88 in co-IP assays.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assay revealed that Vangl2 interacted strongly with IKKα, IKKβ, p65, and MyD88 (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H

claim: Endogenous Vangl2 was strongly associated with p65 upon LPS stimulation in BMDMs, but not with IKKα, IKKβ, or MyD88.
source: In addition, endogenous co-IP immunoblot analyses showed that Vangl2 was strongly associated with p65 upon LPS stimulation in BMDMs, but not with IKKα, IKKβ, or MyD88 (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by endogenous co-IP data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1I

claim: The co-localization between Vangl2 and p65 was notably enhanced upon LPS stimulation.
source: We further investigated the co-localization of Vangl2 and p65 by confocal microscopy and found a weak-co-localization of Vangl2 with p65 in unstimulated cells and the co-localization between Vangl2 and p65 was notably enhanced upon LPS stimulation (Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1K

claim: Vangl2 interacted with p65 mainly in the cytoplasm, although most of Vangl2 located on the membrane.
source: To determine how Vangl2 interacts with cytoplasmic p65, we isolated cytoplasm and membrane in LPS-treated THP-1 cells. We found that Vangl2 interacted with p65 mainly in the cytoplasm, although most of Vangl2 located on the membrane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation and co-IP data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1L

claim: The PkBD domain of Vangl2 is important for the Vangl2–p65 interaction.
source: We found Vangl2 FL (full-length), T2 (ΔNT + TM), T3 (ΔCT), and T4 (ΔNT) interacted with the full-length p65, while Vangl2 T1 (ΔPkBD + CT) abrogated their association (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1M), indicating that the PkBD domain is important for the Vangl2–p65 interaction.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data with Vangl2 deletion mutants shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1M

claim: Deletion of the PkBD domain (T1), but not other domains, of Vangl2 abolished the Vangl2-mediated inhibition of NF-κB-luc activity.
source: Moreover, we observed that deletion of the PkBD domain (T1), but not other domains, of Vangl2 abolished the Vangl2-mediated inhibition of NF-κB-luc activity, and transfection of Vangl2 PkBD domain achieved similar inhibition on p65 induced NF-κB activation as Vangl2 FL did (Figure 3J).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3J

claim: Vangl2 suppresses NF-κB signaling by targeting p65 through Vangl2 PkBD domain interaction.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that Vangl2 suppresses NF-κB signaling by targeting p65 through Vangl2 PkBD domain interaction.
evidence: Inferred from domain mapping and functional assays

claim: Vangl2 dramatically decreased the protein level of p65 in a dose-dependent manner.
source: Next we sought to study the physiological role of Vangl2-p65 interaction in the regulation of NF-κB signaling by transfecting 293T cells with Flag-tagged p65, together with increasing doses of Vangl2, and found that Vangl2 dramatically decreased the protein level of p65 in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The abundance of p65 mRNA did not change in cells with increased expression of Vangl2.
source: To exclude the possibility that the downregulation of p65 protein by Vangl2 was caused by the inhibition of p65 transcription, qPCR results suggested that the abundance of p65 mRNA did not change in cells with increased expression of Vangl2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Vangl2 facilitated the degradation of the p65 phosphorylation mutants.
source: Moreover, Vangl2 facilitated the degradation of the p65 phosphorylation mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: Vangl2 phosphorylation mutants were observed to degrade p65.
source: and Vangl2 phosphorylation mutants were observed to degrade p65 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), indicating that Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation is independent of its phosphorylation status.
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation is independent of p65 phosphorylation status.
source: indicating that Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation is independent of its phosphorylation status.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with phosphorylation mutants

claim: Vangl2 interacted with p65 mainly in the cytoplasm and mediated the degradation of p65 in the cytoplasmic fraction.
source: Since activated p65 translocates to the nucleus, we next assessed whether Vangl2 regulates the degradation of p65 in the cytoplasm or nucleus, and found that the Vangl2 interacted with p65 mainly in the cytoplasm (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and mediated the degradation of p65 in the cytoplasmic fraction (Figure 4C), which is consistent with the result that Vangl2 and p65 co-localized in the cytoplasm (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by cellular fractionation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4C

claim: Vangl2-deficient BMDMs stabilized the expression of endogenous p65 after LPS treatment.
source: To further assess whether Vangl2 regulates the degradation of endogenous p65, we found that Vangl2-deficient BMDMs stabilized the expression of endogenous p65 after LPS treatment (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D

claim: The degradation rate of p65 in Vangl2ΔM BMDMs was slower than that of WT cells after 12 hr of LPS stimulation.
source: After 12 hr of LPS stimulation, the cycloheximide (CHX)-chase assay result showed that the degradation rate of p65 in Vangl2ΔM BMDMs was slower than that of WT cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by CHX-chase assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: Vangl2 promotes p65 protein degradation.
source: Together, these data suggest that Vangl2 promotes p65 protein degradation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple degradation assays

claim: The degradation of p65 induced by Vangl2 was blocked by autolysosome inhibitor chloroquine (CQ) and bafilomycin A1 (Baf A1), or autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA).
source: We found the degradation of p65 induced by Vangl2 was blocked by autolysosome inhibitor chloroquine (CQ) and bafilomycin A1 (Baf A1), or autophagy inhibitor 3-methyladenine (3-MA) (Figure 4E)
evidence: Supported by western blot data with inhibitor treatments shown in Figure 4E

claim: The degradation of p65 induced by Vangl2 was not blocked by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 or caspase-1 inhibitor Z-VAD and VX-765.
source: but not by the proteasome inhibitor MG132 or caspase-1 inhibitor Z-VAD and VX-765 (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by western blot data with inhibitor treatments shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: Vangl2 significantly increased the degradation of p65 during rapamycin-triggered autophagy.
source: Furthermore, Vangl2 significantly increased the degradation of p65 during rapamycin-triggered autophagy (Figure 4F), which suggested that Vangl2 promoted autophagic degradation of p65.
evidence: Supported by western blot data with rapamycin treatment shown in Figure 4F

claim: The degradation of p65 triggered by Vangl2 was almost abrogated in ATG5 and Beclin1 KO cells.
source: To further demonstrate Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation through autophagy, we transfected WT, ATG5, and Beclin1 knockout (KO) 293T cells with Vangl2, and found that the degradation of p65 triggered by Vangl2 was almost abrogated in ATG5 and Beclin1 KO cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in knockout cells shown in Figure 4G

claim: The p65 turnover rates were markedly reduced in ATG5 and Beclin1 KO cells post CHX treatment.
source: The p65 turnover rates were markedly reduced in ATG5 and Beclin1 KO cells post CHX treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting that the impaired autophagy prevented p65 degradation.
evidence: Supported by CHX-chase assay data in knockout cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G

claim: NF-κB activation induced by p65 was rescued in ATG5 and Beclin1 KO cells expressing Vangl2, compared to WT 293T cells.
source: Consistently, NF-κB activation induced by p65 was rescued in ATG5 and Beclin1 KO cells expressing Vangl2, compared to WT 293T cells (Figure 4H, I).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data in knockout cells shown in Figure 4H, I

claim: The co-localization of p65 and LC3B was enhanced following LPS stimulation.
source: In addition, the co-localization of p65 and LC3B was enhanced following LPS stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H

claim: Vangl2 specifically promotes p65 degradation through autophagy.
source: Together, our data suggest that Vangl2 specifically promotes p65 degradation through autophagy.
evidence: Inferred from multiple autophagy-related experiments

claim: Vangl2 strongly interacted with the cargo receptors p62 and NDP52, and slightly associated with NBR1 and Nix.
source: To identify the potential cargo receptor responsible for Vangl2-mediated autophagic degradation of p65, we co-transfected 293T cells with Vangl2 and various cargo receptors, followed by co-IP assay. Result suggested that Vangl2 strongly interacted with the cargo receptors p62 and NDP52, and slightly associated with NBR1 and Nix (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5A

claim: p65 only interacted with the cargo receptors p62 and NDP52.
source: However, p65 only interacted with the cargo receptors p62 and NDP52 (Figure 5B), which is consistent with a recent finding that p62 protein is a Vangl2-binding partner (Puvirajesinghe et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5B and citation to previous work

claim: Vangl2 promoted the association between p65 and NDP52, but did not affect p65–p62 complex.
source: We next attempted to clarify whether p62 or NDP52 is involved in Vangl2-mediated autophagic degradation of p65. Interestingly, we found that Vangl2 promoted the association between p65 and NDP52, but did not affect p65–p62 complex (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Vangl2-mediated degradation of p65 was rescued in NDP52 KO cells, but not in p62 KO cells.
source: Consistently, we found that Vangl2-mediated degradation of p65 was rescued in NDP52 KO cells, but not in p62 KO cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in knockout cells shown in Figure 5D

claim: Deficiency of Vangl2 remarkably attenuated the association of endogenous p65 and NDP52.
source: Endogenous co-IP immunoblot analyses also revealed that deficiency of Vangl2 remarkably attenuated the association of endogenous p65 and NDP52 (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by endogenous co-IP data shown in Figure 5E

claim: NDP52, but not p62, enhanced the association between p65 and Vangl2.
source: Likewise, NDP52, but not p62, enhanced the association between p65 and Vangl2 (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Vangl2 failed to inhibit the activation of NF-κB signaling in NDP52 KO cells.
source: And Vangl2 failed to inhibit the activation of NF-κB signaling in NDP52 KO cells (Figure 5G), but not in p62 KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data in knockout cells shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: The degradation rates of p65 were reduced in NDP52 KO cells, but not in p62 KO cells.
source: Furthermore, compared with WT cells, CHX-chase assay results showed that the degradation rates of p65 were reduced in NDP52 KO cells (Figure 5H), but not in p62 KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by CHX-chase assay data in knockout cells shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Vangl2 mediates the NDP52-directed selective autophagic degradation of p65.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Vangl2 mediates the NDP52-directed selective autophagic degradation of p65.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments with NDP52 knockout and interaction studies

claim: The poly-ubiquitination of p65 was impaired in BMDMs from Vangl2ΔM mice after LPS stimulation, compared to WT mice.
source: To demonstrate this, we performed endogenous co-IP assay and found that the poly-ubiquitination of p65 was impaired in BMDMs from Vangl2ΔM mice after LPS stimulation, compared to WT mice (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by endogenous co-IP data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Vangl2 specifically increased the total and K63-linked (K63-only ubiquitin mutant) poly-ubiquitination of p65.
source: Moreover, Vangl2 specifically increased the total and K63-linked (K63-only ubiquitin mutant) poly-ubiquitination of p65 (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data with ubiquitin mutants shown in Figure 6B

claim: Vangl2 did not affect other ubiquitin linkages (K11, K27, K33, or K48-only ubiquitin mutant) of p65 in an overexpression system.
source: In contrast, Vangl2 did not affect other ubiquitin linkages (K11, K27, K33, or K48-only ubiquitin mutant) of p65 in an overexpression system (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data with ubiquitin mutants shown in Figure 6C

claim: The absence of Vangl2 inhibits K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of p65.
source: To further substantiate the hypothesis that Vangl2 is involved in K63-linked poly-ubiquitinated p65, we conducted a knockdown experiment using small interfering RNA (siRNA) to reduce Vangl2 expression. Our results demonstrated that the absence of Vangl2 inhibits K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of p65 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data with Vangl2 siRNA shown in Figure 6D

claim: Vangl2 promotes the degradation of p65 by promoting the K63-linked ubiquitination of p65.
source: Together, these results suggest that Vangl2 promotes the degradation of p65 by promoting the K63-linked ubiquitination of p65.
evidence: Inferred from ubiquitination experiments

claim: The mRNA level of PDLIM2 and USP7 decreased in Vangl2-deficient BMDMs, compared with WT BMDMs.
source: Here, we found that the mRNA level of PDLIM2 and USP7 decreased in Vangl2-deficient BMDMs, compared with WT BMDMs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–D

claim: Vangl2-mediated inhibition of NF-κB activation and degradation of p65 were blocked by knocking down PDLIM2, but not USP7 or Trim21.
source: To investigate which E3 ubiquitin ligase or DUB is recruited by Vangl2, luciferase assay in Vangl2-expressing 293T cells transfected with scramble, Pdlim2, Usp7, or Trim21 siRNA (Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G) suggested Vangl2-mediated inhibition of NF-κB activation and degradation of p65 were blocked by knocking down PDLIM2, but not USP7 or Trim21 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay and western blot data with siRNA shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E–G

claim: Pdlim2 knockdown in BMDMs resulted in higher expression of Il6 and Il1b in response to LPS stimulation.
source: Meanwhile, Pdlim2 knockdown in BMDMs also resulted in higher expression of Il6 and Il1b in response to LPS stimulation (Figure 7B, C), indicating that PDLIM2 plays a key role in promoting Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation.
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7B, C

claim: PDLIM2 plays a key role in promoting Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation.
source: indicating that PDLIM2 plays a key role in promoting Vangl2-mediated p65 degradation.
evidence: Inferred from siRNA knockdown experiments

claim: Vangl2 interacted with PDLIM2.
source: We next investigated whether Vangl2 promoted the association between p65 and PDLIM2 by co-IP experiments. Our results indicated that Vangl2 interacted with PDLIM2 (Figure 7D)
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Vangl2 promoted the association between p65 and PDLIM2.
source: and promoted the association between p65 and PDLIM2 (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 7E

claim: PDLIM2 accelerated the degradation of p65 in the presence of Vangl2.
source: Notably, PDLIM2 accelerated the degradation of p65 in the presence of Vangl2 (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7F

claim: PDLIM2 deficiency markedly impaired Vangl2-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination of p65.
source: Conversely, PDLIM2 deficiency markedly impaired Vangl2-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination of p65 (Figure 7G)
evidence: Supported by co-IP data with PDLIM2 siRNA shown in Figure 7G

claim: Knockdown of Vangl2 inhibited K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of p65 mediated by PDLIM2.
source: and knockdown of Vangl2 inhibited K63-linked poly-ubiquitination of p65 mediated by PDLIM2 (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data with Vangl2 siRNA shown in Figure 7H

claim: Vangl2 functions as a potential adaptor to recruit E3 ubiquitin ligase PDLIM2 to p65 and promotes the K63-linked ubiquitination of p65 for its subsequent autophagic degradation.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Vangl2 functions as a potential adaptor to recruit E3 ubiquitin ligase PDLIM2 to p65 and promotes the K63-linked ubiquitination of p65 for its subsequent autophagic degradation.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing Vangl2-PDLIM2-p65 interactions and ubiquitination

claim: Vangl2 is widely known for its function in organ development, such as brain, tooth, tongue, and kidney.
source: As a core PCP component, Vangl2 is widely known for its function in organ development, such as brain, tooth, tongue, and kidney (Bailly et al., 2018; Hatakeyama et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 is phosphorylated in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and then transported to the cell surface and becomes stabilized, while the unphosphorylated Vangl2 is unstable and internalized to degrade via the lysosomal pathway.
source: Vangl2 has four transmembrane domains with both carboxyl termini and amino oriented toward the cytoplasm, which is phosphorylated in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and then transported to the cell surface and becomes stabilized, while the unphosphorylated Vangl2 is unstable and internalized to degrade via the lysosomal pathway (Feng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 inhibited matrix metalloproteinase 2 (MMP2) activity and affected cell adhesion to extracellular matrix proteins.
source: Indeed, Vangl2 inhibited matrix metalloproteinase 2 (MMP2) activity and affected cell adhesion to extracellular matrix proteins (Jessen and Jessen, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 modulates glomerular injury by promoting MMP9.
source: Vangl2 also modulates glomerular injury by promoting MMP9 (Papakrivopoulou et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 is markedly downregulated in patients with emphysema.
source: Vangl2 is markedly downregulated in patients with emphysema (Poobalasingam et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 level was upregulated and amplified in breast, ovarian, and uterine carcinomas.
source: while which level was upregulated and amplified in breast, ovarian, and uterine carcinomas (Kandoth et al., 2013; Cerami et al., 2012; Gao et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 is bounded to p62 to promote breast cancer.
source: In addition, Vangl2 is bounded to p62 to promote breast cancer (Puvirajesinghe et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 prevents osteogenic differentiation in mesenchymal stem cells, resulting in osteogenic dysplasia.
source: Our previous study showed that Vangl2 prevents osteogenic differentiation in mesenchymal stem cells, resulting in osteogenic dysplasia (Gong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Vangl2-mediated downstream factors of Toll-like (TLR) or interleukin (IL)-1 receptor, such as myeloid differentiation factor 88 (MyD88).
source: Vangl2-mediated downstream factors of Toll-like (TLR) or interleukin (IL)-1 receptor, such as myeloid differentiation factor 88 (MyD88) (Gong et al., 2021), suggesting that Vangl2 may play roles in immune-related diseases, including autoimmune diseases.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: The NF-κB signaling is critical for the pathogenesis of a number of inflammatory diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and sepsis.
source: The NF-κB signaling is critical for the pathogenesis of a number of inflammatory diseases, such as inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and sepsis (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: NLRC5 strongly prevents NF-κB signaling pathway by interacting with IκB kinase (IKK) α/IKKβ and blocking their phosphorylation.
source: Recent research demonstrated that NLRC5 strongly prevents NF-κB signaling pathway by interacting with IκB kinase (IKK) α/IKKβ and blocking their phosphorylation (Cui et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: COMMD1, PPARγ, SOCS1, and GCN5 were shown to negatively regulate NF-κB signaling.
source: COMMD1, PPARγ, SOCS1, and GCN5 were also shown to negatively regulate NF-κB signaling (Bartuzi et al., 2013; Mao et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Trim21 enhanced the interaction of p65 with IKK, which promotes p65 phosphorylation and downstream gene activation.
source: Meanwhile, tripartite motif-containing protein 21 (Trim21) enhanced the interaction of p65 with IKK, which promotes p65 phosphorylation and downstream gene activation (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Autophagy is a conserved intracellular degradation pathway that decomposes cytoplasmic organelles and components, and acts as a defense mechanism to pathogen infection.
source: Autophagy, a conserved intracellular degradation pathway, decomposes cytoplasmic organelles and components, and acts as a defense mechanism to pathogen infection, playing a crucial role in nutrient recycling, stress response, and cellular homeostasis (Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013; Denton and Kumar, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: Selective autophagy targets immune regulators for degradation, thus suppressing innate immune signaling, such as type I IFN and NF-κB signaling.
source: Selective autophagy targets immune regulators for degradation, thus suppressing innate immune signaling, such as type I IFN and NF-κB signaling (Pradel et al., 2020; Tong et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature

claim: p62 protein has been identified as a novel Vangl2-binding partner.
source: Moreover, p62 protein has been identified as a novel Vangl2-binding partner (Puvirajesinghe et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature

claim: Vangl2 reduces lysosomal chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) activity by targeting LAMP-2A for degradation.
source: and our recent study has demonstrated that Vangl2 reduces lysosomal chaperone-mediated autophagy (CMA) activity by targeting LAMP-2A for degradation (Gong et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors

claim: Vangl2 functions as a 'molecular brake' in the negative regulation of NF-κB signaling to prevent excessive and potentially harmful immune responses during sepsis.
source: In this study, we uncover a previously unrecognized role of Vangl2, as a 'molecular brake', in the negative regulation of NF-κB signaling to prevent excessive and potentially harmful immune responses during sepsis in both human patient samples and LPS-induced mouse model.
evidence: Inferred from the overall findings of the study

claim: Induction of Vangl2 upon inflammation recruits an E3 ubiquitin ligase PDLIM2 to catalyze K63-linked ubiquitination on p65.
